days.title: DNA Replication — Steps & Enzymes
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the steps of DNA replication.
  • Identify enzymes involved.
  • Explain semi-conservative replication.
  • Diagram the replication fork.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Semi-conservative — each new DNA has one old + one new strand.
  • Replication fork — the Y-shaped region where DNA unwinds.
  • Helicase — unwinds DNA.
  • DNA polymerase — adds nucleotides.
  • Ligase — seals fragments.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Steps of Replication

  1. Initiation: Helicase unwinds DNA at origin of replication
  2. Elongation: Primase lays RNA primer; DNA polymerase adds nucleotides (5'→3')
  3. Lagging strand: Made in Okazaki fragments
  4. Termination: Ligase seals fragments; two identical DNA molecules result

B. Enzymes Summary

EnzymeFunction
HelicaseUnwinds double helix
PrimaseSynthesizes RNA primer
DNA polymeraseAdds DNA nucleotides
LigaseSeals Okazaki fragments

💬 Let's Discuss

Every time a cell divides, all of its DNA — about 3 billion base pairs in a human cell — must be copied accurately in a few hours. DNA replication happens during the S phase of interphase.

Replication is semi-conservative: the two strands separate, and each serves as a template for a new strand. Each new DNA molecule therefore has one old strand and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl proved this in 1958 using heavy and light nitrogen.

A team of enzymes does the work. Helicase unwinds and unzips the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds, forming a Y-shaped replication fork. Primase lays down a short RNA primer, because DNA polymerase cannot start a strand from nothing. DNA polymerase adds DNA nucleotides that pair with the template (A–T, G–C), and also proofreads its work, making only about one error per billion bases. Finally, DNA ligase seals gaps in the sugar–phosphate backbone, acting like glue.

One complication: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the 5' → 3' direction. Since the strands are antiparallel, one new strand — the leading strand — is made continuously toward the fork. The other, the lagging strand, must be made backward in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, each with its own primer. The primers are later replaced with DNA, and ligase joins the fragments.

Think of copying a zipper: helicase opens it, primase marks where to start, polymerase adds the new teeth, and ligase stitches the pieces together.

Common mistake: saying ligase "unzips" DNA. Helicase unwinds; ligase joins.

pairs.why: Semi-conservative: each new DNA keeps one original strand.
The replication fork is the Y-shaped region where strands separate.
Helicase unwinds the double helix.
Primase makes the short RNA primer.
DNA polymerase adds complementary DNA nucleotides.
Ligase joins Okazaki fragments into one strand.
Okazaki fragments are short pieces made on the lagging strand.

scenarios.explanation: Unwinding the helix is helicase's job.
The RNA primer is made by primase.
DNA polymerase adds nucleotides.

scenarios.text: Fragments on the lagging strand are sealed.
scenarios.explanation: Ligase seals fragments on the lagging strand.
Each new DNA has one old and one new strand — semi-conservative.

scenarios.text: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides in which direction?
scenarios.explanation: DNA polymerase builds strands only 5' → 3'.

questions.text: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix?
questions.explanation: Helicase unwinds the DNA double helix.

choices.label: One old and one new strand

questions.explanation: Semi-conservative means each new DNA has one old and one new strand.
Ligase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments.

takeaways: Helicase unwinds, primase lays primer, polymerase adds nucleotides, ligase seals.
Leading strand is continuous; lagging strand is in Okazaki fragments.

days.title: Transcription — DNA to mRNA
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the process of transcription.
  • Identify the role of RNA polymerase.
  • Explain mRNA processing.
  • Diagram the flow from DNA to mRNA.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Transcription — DNA → mRNA.
  • RNA polymerase — enzyme that makes mRNA.
  • Template strand — the DNA strand read by RNA polymerase.
  • Codon — 3 nucleotides coding for an amino acid.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Steps of Transcription

  1. Initiation: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter
  2. Elongation: RNA polymerase reads the template strand and adds RNA nucleotides
  3. Termination: RNA polymerase reaches the terminator; mRNA is released

B. mRNA Processing (Eukaryotes)

  • 5' cap added
  • Poly-A tail added
  • Introns removed (splicing)
  • Exons joined

C. DNA → mRNA Example

DNA: TAC GGA TTC → mRNA: AUG CCU AAG

💬 Let's Discuss

Transcription is the first step of gene expression: a gene's DNA is copied into messenger RNA (mRNA). In eukaryotes it happens in the nucleus. Only one gene (a short region) is copied at a time, and only one DNA strand — the template strand — is read.

It happens in three stages. 1. Initiation: the enzyme RNA polymerase binds to a promoter, a DNA sequence just before the gene (often containing a "TATA box") that signals "start here." It unwinds a short stretch of DNA. 2. Elongation: RNA polymerase moves along the template, adding complementary RNA nucleotides. Remember that RNA uses U instead of T: template A → U, T → A, G → C, C → G. Unlike DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase needs no primer. 3. Termination: at a terminator sequence, the polymerase releases the new RNA.

Practice: template DNA TAC GGA → mRNA AUG CCU.

In eukaryotes, the first RNA (pre-mRNA) is processed before leaving the nucleus. A 5' cap is added to the front and a poly-A tail to the end; these protect the mRNA and help ribosomes recognize it. Then splicing removes non-coding introns and joins the coding exons (remember: exons are expressed, introns stay in). One gene can be spliced in different ways, so it can produce several proteins — one reason humans make far more proteins than their roughly 20,000 genes.

Common mistake: writing T in the mRNA. RNA never contains thymine; A on the template always becomes U.

pairs.why: Transcription copies a DNA gene into mRNA.
RNA polymerase builds the mRNA strand.
The promoter is where RNA polymerase binds to start.
The terminator signals the end of transcription.
Eukaryotic mRNA receives a protective 5' cap.
Splicing removes introns and joins exons.

scenarios.explanation: RNA polymerase binding at the promoter is initiation.
Adding RNA nucleotides is elongation.
Reaching the terminator is termination.
Removing introns is part of mRNA processing.
T→A, A→U, C→G: TAC becomes AUG.
G→C, G→C, A→U: GGA becomes CCU.

questions.text: Where does transcription occur in eukaryotes?
questions.explanation: In eukaryotes, transcription occurs in the nucleus.

questions.text: If DNA has TAC, mRNA has:
questions.explanation: T→A, A→U, C→G, so TAC becomes AUG.

takeaways: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter.
mRNA is processed in eukaryotes (cap, tail, splicing).

days.title: Translation — mRNA to Protein
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the process of translation.
  • Explain the roles of mRNA, tRNA, and rRNA.
  • Use the codon table.
  • Diagram protein synthesis.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Translation — mRNA → protein.
  • tRNA — brings amino acids to ribosome.
  • Anticodon — pairs with mRNA codon.
  • Ribosome — site of translation.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Steps of Translation

  1. Initiation: Ribosome binds mRNA at the start codon (AUG)
  2. Elongation: tRNA brings amino acids; peptide bonds form
  3. Termination: Stop codon reached; polypeptide released

B. Codon Table

  • AUG = Methionine (start)
  • UAA, UAG, UGA = Stop
  • 20 amino acids encoded by 64 codons

C. Example

mRNA: AUG CCU AAG → Met–Pro–Lys

💬 Let's Discuss

Translation converts the mRNA's code into a chain of amino acids at the ribosome. Three kinds of RNA work together: mRNA carries the codons, tRNA carries amino acids, and rRNA forms the ribosome and links amino acids together.

Each tRNA has a three-base anticodon at one end and its matching amino acid at the other. The anticodon pairs with a complementary codon on the mRNA (codon AUG ↔ anticodon UAC), so each amino acid is placed in the right order — tRNA acts as the translator between the two "languages."

1. Initiation: the small ribosomal subunit binds the mRNA and finds the start codon AUG, which codes for methionine (Met). The first tRNA binds, and the large subunit joins. 2. Elongation: tRNAs bring amino acids codon by codon; the ribosome forms peptide bonds between them and moves along the mRNA, three bases at a time. 3. Termination: when a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA) is reached, no tRNA matches; a release factor frees the finished polypeptide, which then folds into its shape.

Reading a codon chart: mRNA AUG CCU AAG → Met – Pro – Lys. Always read from the start codon, in groups of three, without skipping or overlapping.

Several ribosomes can translate the same mRNA at once (a polysome), so a cell can make many copies of a protein quickly. Some antibiotics, like tetracycline and streptomycin, kill bacteria by jamming their ribosomes.

Common mistake: using the DNA sequence or the anticodon to look up amino acids. The codon chart is read using mRNA codons.

pairs.why: Translation builds a protein from mRNA instructions.
tRNA carries specific amino acids to the ribosome.
The anticodon on tRNA pairs with the mRNA codon.
Ribosomes are the site of translation.
AUG starts translation and codes for methionine.
UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.

scenarios.explanation: Binding at AUG is initiation.
tRNAs adding amino acids is elongation.
Reaching a stop codon is termination.
AUG = Met, CCU = Pro, AAG = Lys.
UAA is a stop codon.
AUG is the start codon (methionine).

questions.text: Which molecule brings amino acids to the ribosome?
questions.explanation: tRNA brings amino acids to the ribosome.
Translation takes place at the ribosome.

takeaways: mRNA is read in codons (3 nucleotides).
tRNA brings amino acids; anticodon pairs with codon.
AUG = start; UAA, UAG, UGA = stop.

days.title: Mutations & Their Effects
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define genetic mutation.
  • Differentiate gene mutations from chromosomal mutations.
  • Describe effects of mutations.
  • Relate mutations to genetic disorders.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Mutation — change in DNA sequence.
  • Point mutation — single nucleotide change.
  • Frameshift — insertion/deletion shifts reading frame.
  • Chromosomal mutation — changes in chromosome structure or number.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Types of Point Mutations

TypeEffect
SilentNo change in amino acid
MissenseDifferent amino acid
NonsensePremature stop codon

B. Frameshift Mutations

  • Insertion or deletion of nucleotides
  • Shifts the reading frame
  • Usually more severe

C. Chromosomal Mutations

  • Deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation
  • Aneuploidy (e.g., Down syndrome)

💬 Let's Discuss

A mutation is any change in the DNA sequence. Mutations can happen by chance during replication or be caused by mutagens such as UV light, X-rays, tobacco smoke and some chemicals.

Point mutations (substitutions) change a single base. Their effect depends on the codon: Silent — the new codon still codes for the same amino acid (GAA and GAG are both glutamic acid), so the protein is unchanged. Missense — a different amino acid is coded. In sickle-cell anemia, one A→T change makes valine replace glutamic acid in hemoglobin, changing the protein's shape. Nonsense — the codon becomes a stop codon, so the protein is cut short and usually useless.

Frameshift mutations are insertions or deletions of bases (not in multiples of three). Because codons are read in threes, every codon after the change is shifted. Try it with a sentence: THE CAT ATE THE RAT → delete one letter → THE ATA TET HER AT. Frameshifts usually wreck the whole protein.

Chromosomal mutations affect large segments: deletion (segment lost), duplication (segment repeated), inversion (segment reversed) and translocation (segment moved to another chromosome). Changes in chromosome number, called aneuploidy (like trisomy 21), result from nondisjunction.

Not all mutations are harmful. Many are neutral, and a few are beneficial — mutations are the original source of all genetic variation and fuel evolution. Mutations in body cells affect only that person (and may cause cancer); mutations in gametes can be inherited.

Common mistake: thinking every mutation causes disease. Silent mutations change nothing.

pairs.why: A mutation is any change in the DNA sequence.
A point mutation changes one nucleotide.
A silent mutation does not change the amino acid.
A missense mutation codes for a different amino acid.
A nonsense mutation creates an early stop codon.
Inserting or deleting bases shifts the reading frame.

scenarios.text: A single nucleotide change has no effect.
scenarios.explanation: No change in the amino acid is a silent mutation.

scenarios.text: A single nucleotide change causes a different amino acid.
scenarios.explanation: A different amino acid is a missense mutation.

scenarios.text: A mutation creates a premature stop codon.
scenarios.explanation: An early stop codon is a nonsense mutation.
Inserting one base shifts the reading frame — frameshift.
An extra whole chromosome is aneuploidy.
A segment flipped in reverse is an inversion.

questions.text: A mutation that does NOT change the amino acid is:
questions.explanation: A silent mutation leaves the amino acid unchanged.

questions.text: A frameshift mutation is caused by:
A premature stop codon results from which mutation?
questions.explanation: A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon.

takeaways: Chromosomal mutations include aneuploidy, inversion, translocation.
